opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one I think about a lot now that I'm advising students myself.

The first thing I'd say is: don't rush to pick a direction too early. When you're starting out, your job is to build taste. Taste in research means being able to look at a problem and sense whether it's important, whether it's tractable, and whether you're the right person to work on it. You can't really learn that from reading a list of hot topics. You develop it by working on real problems, getting your hands dirty, failing a few times, and seeing which ideas end up mattering a few years later.

The second thing is fundamentals. In robotics and AI, the field moves incredibly fast. What's trendy this year might look very different in three years. But the basics don't change that much: linear algebra, probability, optimization, control, and solid engineering skills. If you have those, you can pick up whatever the new paradigm is, whether it's large models, diffusion policies, or something none of us has thought of yet. If you only chase the trend, you're always one step behind.

Third, I'd encourage people to seek exposure to both worlds if they can. Doing an internship in industry during your PhD, or collaborating with industry labs, teaches you things academia doesn't, like what problems actually show up when you try to deploy something at scale and what resources it takes. Academia gives you something industry often doesn't: the freedom to work on long-horizon, risky ideas that may not pay off for five or ten years. Once you've seen both, the choice becomes much less abstract. You can ask yourself, "Which kind of problem do I want to wake up thinking about?"

And finally, find good mentors and good peers. A lot of my own thinking was shaped by the people around me during my PhD and afterward, people who pushed me to ask, "Why does this matter?" instead of just "Can I get this to work?" That question, why does this matter, is really the foundation. If you keep asking it honestly, the direction tends to reveal itself, whether that ends up being in industry or academia.

r001.rationale: The response advises students to build research taste early by judging whether problems are important, tractable, and suited to them.

r002.rationale: It recommends working on real problems, but does not recommend relatively full-stack projects or explain how they build understanding of the whole system.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, partly because I've lived on both sides of it, going from a PhD and industry research back into academia.

The honest answer is that you can't really choose a direction well until you've built enough taste to know what a good problem looks like, and taste comes from doing, not from reading. So the first thing I'd tell a young researcher is: get your hands dirty early. Pick a problem, even a small one, go end to end on it, and ship something. Reimplement a paper, break it, figure out why it breaks. You learn far more about where a field is actually stuck from one failed experiment than from twenty papers that claim everything works.

The second thing is to be deliberate about what you're optimizing for in each phase. Early on, breadth matters more than impact. Try a few different sub-areas, work with a few different people, and pay attention to what you find yourself thinking about in the shower. That signal is real. The problems you can't stop poking at are usually the ones you'll do your best work on, and they're also the ones that will sustain you when the project hits its inevitable two-year valley.

Third, and this is the one people underrate: find your reference frame. Your advisor, your collaborators, the people whose work you admire. Those people shape your standards for what counts as interesting and what counts as rigorous. If you surround yourself with people who only chase benchmarks, you'll learn to chase benchmarks. If you're around people who ask "why does this work" and "what would make this not work," you'll learn to ask that too. Choosing who you learn from is often more consequential than choosing what you work on.

On the industry versus academia question specifically, I'd push back a little on treating it as a binary you have to resolve early. The skills transfer more than people think. What differs is the time horizon and the constraints. In industry you get resources and real problems, but the direction is partly set for you. In academia you get freedom, but you have to generate your own conviction and often work with a tenth of the compute. Spend time in both if you can, even as an intern, because knowing which set of constraints energizes you rather than drains you is something you can only find out by experiencing it.

And last thing: don't confuse choosing a direction with locking one in. In robotics and learning, the field has reinvented itself every few years. The researchers I most admire didn't pick the right direction in year one. They built a core set of skills and a way of thinking about problems, and then they were able to pivot when the landscape shifted. So build the foundation, stay curious, and let the direction emerge from the work rather than trying to decide it in advance.

r001.rationale: The response recommends building research taste through hands-on work, but does not clearly say to form independent judgments about what one believes.

r002.rationale: It recommends picking a problem early, taking it end to end, and shipping something, which communicates doing a full project to understand the whole system.

astra-6.text:
I think early on, it’s useful to focus less on deciding between industry and academia and more on developing your ability to do research. Can you identify a meaningful problem, understand what’s already been tried, and design an experiment that helps you learn something—even when it doesn’t work?

One way to build that foundation is to work closely with people you can learn from and take a project far enough that you experience the whole process. Reading papers is important, but actually trying to make an idea work gives you a different understanding of the field and of yourself. You start to discover which questions you keep coming back to and what kind of work you enjoy.

If you have opportunities to experience different environments through internships or collaborations, take them. Pay attention to the mentorship, the way problems are chosen, and the day-to-day work. You don’t need to have your entire career mapped out. Build the skills and judgment that let you make a more informed choice as you go.

r001.rationale: The response encourages noticing which questions the researcher returns to and what work they enjoy, but it does not clearly recommend forming independent judgments about what they believe as early as possible.

r002.rationale: The response recommends taking a project far enough to experience the whole process, which communicates undertaking a relatively full-stack project early in research training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think early on, it’s important to build a strong foundation while keeping an open mind about where you want to go. Learn the fundamentals, but also get your hands dirty with research. Often, you don’t really understand what interests you until you’ve worked on a problem long enough to encounter the frustrating parts.

I’d encourage young researchers to experience different environments if they can—work with different mentors, collaborate with people outside their immediate area, and try an industry internship. Pay attention to what motivates you. Do you enjoy formulating questions, building systems, or getting something to work for real users? Those experiences give you a much better basis for choosing than the labels “industry” and “academia.”

And don’t feel that you need to identify your lifelong research direction right away. Develop the ability to learn deeply, ask good questions, and follow through on a project. That foundation gives you room to change direction as your interests evolve.

r001.rationale: The response encourages noticing what motivates you, but it does not clearly recommend forming independent judgments about what you believe or developing research taste early.
